power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. text.text: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups.
Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors.
However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce.
We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals.
B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection.
We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guidedrespiration tasks.

Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection.
B3 derived HR and HRV closely matched reference measures across tasks, with high quality ECG recordings and minimal data loss, except during vigorous arm swinging.
Respiratory rate and pattern metrics, including exhalation peak timing, also showed strong agreement.
The B3 thermistor accurately tracked respiration rate even at higher breathing frequencies, although minor timing offsets occurred during some guided respiration segments.

Overall, B3 performed comparably to the reference system for cardiac and respiratory measures, offering an affordable, open-source solution for physiological monitoring in real-world interactive settings.
Imagine a few dozen people dancing to music in a park, while researchers wirelessly and reliably measure their heartbeats, respiration and electrodermal response.
Imagine a concert hall where fifty or so spectators' emotional states are tracked in parallel for offline analysis.
Physiological signals, including heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), and respiration, offer researchers a powerful lens through which to study human behavior and health.

Cardiac and respiratory measures have long been used to monitor stress (Faust, Hagiwara, Hong, Lih, & Acharya, 2018; Kim, Cheon, Bai, Lee, & Koo, 2018; Pourmohammadi & Maleki, 2020), cognitive load (Ayres, Lee, Paas, & Van Merrienboer, 2021; Hidalgo-Muñoz et al., 2019), emotional states (Harmat et al., 2015; Jerritta, Murugappan, Nagarajan, & Wan, 2011; Zhang, Chen, Zhan, Yang, & Xia, 2017), and physical exertion (Nicolò, Massaroni, Schena, & Sacchetti, 2020) giving researchers the ability to objectively assess various psychophysiological states.

text.text: For instance, acute mental stress is typically associated with increased HR and respiration rate, together with reduced HRV.
The latter phenomenon is generally interpreted as reflecting reduced vagal/parasympathetic influence (Widjaja, Orini, Vlemincx, & Van Huffel, 2013).

text.text: Beyond applications focused on individual physiological states, there is growing interest in studying physiological processes at the group level, particularly in research on interpersonal dynamics and music cognition (Delius & Müller, 2023; Gugnowska et al., 2022; Lange et al., 2022).

text.text: Notably, physiological variables such as HR and HRV become in some cases synchronized in individuals during joint action, providing insight into emotional and collaborative dynamics (Danyluck & Page-Gould, 2019; Gordon et al., 2020; Palumbo et al., 2017; Thorson, West, & Mendes, 2018).

text.text: To enable such applications, an essential first step is to ensure that individual cardiac and respiratory signals can be recorded accurately under conditions approximating real interactive settings.
Accurately capturing cardiac (HR, HRV) and respiratory signals is critical in both laboratory and field studies.
Traditionally, researchers have relied on off-the-shelf wired and wireless physiological recording systems from vendors such as ADInstruments (Dunedin, New Zealand), BIOPAC Systems, Inc.
(Goleta, CA, USA), and BioSemi B.V. (Amsterdam, the Netherlands).
In highly mobile or interactive paradigms, wired configurations can restrict participants' freedom of movement because of cables and bulky hardware, thereby reducing ecological validity.

Wireless systems alleviate some of these constraints; however, many still depend on a central acquisition module connected to a personal computer (PC), which limits portability and complicates their use in naturalistic settings outside the laboratory.
In recent years, a variety of portable and wearable physiology monitors have emerged, providing greater flexibility while maintaining research-grade data quality.
A comparison of available platforms is provided in the accompanying https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/GX6W3  (Bahadori, Voix, Dalla Bella, & van Vugt, 2024).

text.text: For example, a validation study of the Shimmer wearable sensor platform (Shimmer Research Ltd., Dublin, Ireland) showed that its electrocardiographic (ECG), electromyographic (EMG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) signals closely matched those recorded using standard laboratory equipment (Burns et al., 2010).

text.text: Similarly, the Polar H10 heart rate sensor (Polar Electro Oy, Kempele, Finland) has been shown to produce HRV metrics that agree with those derived from standard ECG recordings (Schaffarczyk, Rogers, Reer, & Gronwald, 2022).

text.text: The Empatica wristband (Empatica Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA) has also demonstrated the ability to capture heart rate and HRV accurately under controlled, low-motion conditions, offering an unobtrusive alternative to wired systems (Schuurmans et al., 2020).

text.text: Collectively, these systems illustrate the range of tools now available for physiological data acquisition, from traditional wired setups to modern wireless wearables.
Despite these advances in wearable technology, many current solutions remain proprietary.
High equipment costs can restrict the number of units that can be purchased for simultaneous recording, thereby limiting achievable group sizes and the statistical power of group-based studies.

Proprietary hardware and software may also constrain researchers' ability to modify the system, integrate additional sensors or data streams, and develop experimental paradigms beyond those anticipated by the manufacturer.

This limitation is particularly relevant to studies of interpersonal dynamics and music cognition, where synchronized audio recordings of speech or musical performance may be essential alongside physiological signals. (see the OSF repository for available platforms (Bahadori et al., 2024)).

text.text: Finally, many available systems, including commercial ones, have not been subjected to stress tests under conditions which do not require that the participant sit absolutely still.
As a result, their reliability in more naturalistic settings, where participants can move, talk, and interact, remains insufficiently documented.

To evaluate the utility of B3 for rigorous scientific research, the device was benchmarked against BioNomadix from BIOPAC, a widely used commercial research-grade physiological recording system (Babusiak, Hajducik, Medvecky, Lukac, & Klarak, 2021; Flagler, Tong, Allison, & Wilcox, 2020).

text.text: ECG and respiratory signals were recorded simultaneously with both systems on the same set of participants while they performed tasks varying in motor involvement, including rest, voice production, walking, arm-swing movements, and guided respiration at different rates.

The analyses compared (1) the proportion of usable data collected during each task, (2) HR and HRV, with HRV indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), and (3) respiratory signal usability, respiration rate, and the accuracy and consistency of detected respiratory events.
In the guided-respiration task, the pacing cue provided a ground-truth reference for expected respiration rate and timing, allowing calculation of the absolute measurement error.
Nine participants were recruited for this study (7 females; age range, 23-46 years; mean ± std, 30.6 ± 6.3 years).

The experimental protocol adhered to the principles of the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki and received approval from the Ethics Committee for Research in Education and Psychology at the University of Montreal (CEREP-22-007-D).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
The B3 system is an ambulatory hardware-software platform that enables the simultaneous recording and streaming of cardiac, respiratory, movement, and audio data using a compact wireless device.
Cardiac activity is recorded through electrocardiography (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG), which captures changes in peripheral blood volume.

Respiratory activity is recorded using a respiration belt and a thermistor; movement is captured through a three-dimensional (3D) accelerometer; and ambient sound is recorded using a mono omnidirectional electret microphone.
Physiological and movement signals are sampled at 500 Hz, whereas audio is sampled at 48 kHz.
All data streams are synchronized (Figure 1A).

text.text: The computational core consists of a Teensy 4.1 development board (PJRC, Sherwood, OR, USA), operating at 600 MHz, which interfaces with the onboard sensors through serial peripheral interface (SPI), inter-integrated circuit (I²C), inter-IC sound (I²S), universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART), Secure Digital input/output (SDIO), and digital and analog connections.

Acquired data is passed to an ESP32-S3 system-on-chip used as a coprocessor (Espressif Systems The B3 supports two concurrent acquisition modes: a real-time streaming mode via Lab Streaming Layer and local recording mode, saving data to an SD card.

Streaming is available for all data channels except audio and enables real-time inspection of signal quality, whereas all channels are continuously stored on the SD card for subsequent offline analysis.
Streaming can be enabled or disabled without interrupting SD-card recording.

The same BIOPAC unit was used for all nine participants, whereas three separate B3 units with identical designs, architectures, and settings were each tested in three participants to assess interunit consistency.
The experiment began with a 30-second stationary rest block, during which participants stood still and remained silent.
This block established a stationary reference before the first active task.

Equivalent 30-second rest blocks were inserted between the active tasks (hereafter referred to as "rest") to separate consecutive task periods and to provide local reference segments for detecting task-related audio and acceleration activity.

text.text: In this task, they were asked to either speak freely about a random subject or, if they felt comfortable, to speak and sing the "Happy Birthday" song.
Hereafter, this task is referred to as "voice" and each participant performed it twice, with rest in between.

The walking task (here after referred as "walk") required participants to walk continuously around the available space in the experimental room while synchronizing their steps to a metronome set at 90 beats per minute.

The third task (here after referred as "swing") was designed as a movement stress test, using large, repetitive upper-body movements to challenge signal acquisition and evaluate the robustness of the B3 recordings under motion-related perturbations.

Participants started with their arms alongside the body and first performed the movement in a posterior-to-anterior direction: the arms moved backward behind the body, then upward through an overhead position, then forward in front of the body before returning to the starting position alongside the body.
The movement was paced by a metronome set at 45 beats per minute.
After 30 seconds, participants were asked to reverse the direction of the movement and continue.
The fourth task involved a guided respiration (hereafter referred to as "resp") exercise.

In this task, participants viewed a video in which a blue circle on a grey background periodically expanded (accompanied by a high-pitched click) to signal inhalation onset and contracted (accompanied by a low-pitched click) to signal exhalation onset.
Participants were instructed to inhale during circle expansion and exhale during contraction, synchronizing their respiration with the visual cue.
Each exhalation lasted three times longer than each inhalation.
Five respiration rates (4, 5, 6, 10, and 14 breaths per minute [bpm]) were presented in randomized order, each in a separate 90-second block.

text.text: Indeed, because the pacing cue was strictly periodic and participants were instructed to synchronize their breathing with it, detected exhalation onsets were expressed as phase within each paced respiration cycle.
The circular mean phase quantified timing bias (accuracy) relative to the cue, whereas the resultant vector length quantified the consistency of exhalation timing.
For each block, the guided respiration cycle duration (T = 60/bpm) was used, the rate at which participants ought to be breathing if they perfectly followed the guide.

Phases were then shifted by -π/2 so that the expected exhalation onset corresponded to 0 radians.

In this study, the open-source B3 device demonstrated measurement performance comparable to the widely used BIOPAC BioNomadix system for both ECG and respiratory signals.
B3 could accurately measure HR and HRV across a range of activities ranging from resting and speaking to moderate exercise including walking and arm swings.

No statistically significant differences in mean HR or HRV were found between the two systems in almost any task conditions, indicating that B3 can reliably capture cardiac dynamics even during mild physical activity.

This strong agreement in HR metrics mirrors prior observations that modern wearable or low-cost devices can accurately track heart rate, with minimal error relative to ECG references (Stone et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This strong agreement in HR metrics mirrors prior observations that modern wearable or low-cost devices can accurately track heart rate, with minimal error relative to ECG references <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Stone et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, both devices produced very little artefactual ECG data: even during movement tasks, signal quality was largely maintained, and only the vigorous swing task introduced a slight increase in noise for the B3 recordings.
Indeed, both devices were quite similar in finding the HR and HRV in the portions that were considered in the calculations.

This outcome is encouraging, especially as HRV (and RMSSD) is a sensitive measure of autonomic function; the B3's ability to capture RMSSD suggests it successfully detects beat-to-beat intervals with high fidelity.

Such parity in HRV measurement is likely due to B3's direct ECG sensing, unlike some wearables that rely on PPG and show degraded HRV accuracy (Langevin et al., 2021), an ECG-based open device like B3 can achieve research-grade precision in inter-beat interval detection.

text.text: Respiratory measurements from the B3 closely followed those from the reference BIOPAC system.
The B3 is equipped with a flexible respiration belt sensor (recording chest expansion) and a nasal thermistor (recording airflow temperature changes), providing two modalities to capture respiration.
Both of these B3 sensors showed close agreement with BIOPAC respiration signals in terms of respiratory rate and timing.
Across all tasks, respiration rates measured by B3 were similar to those obtained with BIOPAC, and the pattern of inhalations and exhalations aligned closely across devices.
The agreement also extended to the timing of exhalation events.
During natural respiration and most guided respiration segments, peaks corresponding to exhalations in B3's recordings occurred close to those observed in the BIOPAC data.
This indicates that B3 can accurately track the dynamics of respiration cycles, which is essential for applications like stress monitoring or cardiorespiratory research.
In particular, the B3 thermistor sensor performed very well at higher respiration frequencies.
The sensor continued to detect each breath without dropouts or missed peaks, while maintaining accurate counts of breaths per minute.
This is remarkable because some respiratory monitoring modalities, such as inductive belts or PPG-based respiration estimates, can be less reliable at fast respiration rates.
By contrast, thermistors can capture rapid airflow changes reliably when properly calibrated (Ermer, Brewer, Orr, Egan, & Johnson, 2019).
text.formatted: By contrast, thermistors can capture rapid airflow changes reliably when properly calibrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Ermer, Brewer, Orr, Egan, & Johnson, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the B3 thermistor (B3T) generally outperformed the belt sensors in both devices in terms of data usability, particularly during tasks involving movement.

Taken together, the respiration results demonstrate that B3's open hardware approach does not compromise on signal quality: it can measure respiration as effectively as a laboratory-grade system, providing both rate information and close timing of respiratory phases.
While B3 displayed very similar performance to the reference system (BIOPAC), a few minor discrepancies merit discussion.
First, during the swing task, the B3's ECG channel showed a slightly higher level of high-frequency noise and sporadic signal artifact compared to the BIOPAC.
This difference is likely due to motion artifacts -the physical jostling of electrodes and movement-induced muscle electrical activity that contaminate the ECG trace (Kher, Pawar, & Thakar, 2013).
text.formatted: This difference is likely due to motion artifacts -the physical jostling of electrodes and movement-induced muscle electrical activity that contaminate the ECG trace <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kher, Pawar, & Thakar, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Arm swinging involves repetitive shoulder and torso movement, which can tug on leads or generate electromyographic noise.

The BIOPAC BioNomadix, may employ advanced shielded cables, high-quality amplifiers, and sophisticated filtering to mitigate motion artifacts, whereas the B3 -a prototype and lower-cost open-source device -might have more basic shielding or filtering.
Despite these factors, B3 retained a high portion of analyzable ECG data during arm swings, and the derived HR and HRV remained comparable to those obtained with BIOPAC.

This resilience suggests that the B3's design is sufficiently robust for moderate activity, though future improvements, including improved motion artifact filtering algorithms or accelerometer-based noise cancellation could further enhance signal quality in high-motion scenarios.

This outcome shows that, for most practical purposes, the B3's ECG is functionally very close to the reference system (BIOPAC) ECG even when the person being measured is in motion, as they may often be during real-world physiological monitoring.
A slight temporal offset was observed in the B3 thermistor signal during some guided-respiration blocks.

Specifically, during some segments of slower guided respiration, the peaks corresponding to exhalations in the B3 thermistor trace appeared earlier than those observed in the BIOPAC and B3 belt signals.
Several factors could explain this lag.
One possibility is the difference in sensor modality and placement: the BIOPAC likely used a respiratory inductance plethysmography belt, which measures chest expansion directly.

In contrast, the B3 thermistor detected temperature changes of air flow at the nostrils; This suggests that the thermistor's placement and mechanism allow it to capture the onset of airflow at the source, whereas the BIOPAC system's respiratory belt measures a downstream mechanical response.

In particular, the B3T's nasal thermistor directly senses the temperature change of exhaled air at the nostrils (Sabil et al., 2019), providing an immediate proxy for airflow, while the BIOPAC respiratory inductance plethysmography belt monitors chest wall expansion and contraction (i.e., changes in thoracic volume) (Sabil et al., 2019).

text.text: However, the observed offset was small and consistent.
It did not affect breath counting nor the estimated respiration rate, but only the temporal alignment of the exhalation peaks.
Such a discrepancy is likely inconsequential for most research applications.

Yet, it should be taken into account when the precise timing of respiratory phases relative to another time reference matters, particularly when comparing airflow-based measurements with measures of chest-volume change.

Altogether, aside from this timing difference, the B3 thermistor's performance was robust, even under the challenging condition of guided respiration where participants rapidly inhale and exhale on a cue.
The accuracy of B3 in capturing respiration rate and timing pattern, despite using different sensor types (belt vs. thermistor), underscores the reliability of its design.

This also demonstrates how multiple sensors on an open-source device can be combined to cross-validate and enrich respiratory monitoring, for example by integrating both chestmovement and airflow signals to detect apnea or irregular respiration.
The present validation of the B3 device has significant implications for physiological research and health monitoring.

B3's performance, comparable to that of an widely used commercial system, points to the possibility of obtaining high-quality biosignal data without relying exclusively on expensive, proprietary platforms.

These findings support a growing body of evidence that low-cost, open-source biosensing platforms can achieve research-grade accuracy, effectively lowering barriers to entry for laboratory and field researchers (Wagner, Plácido da Silva, & Gramann, 2021).

text.text: This democratization of technology is crucial.

Traditional research equipment like BIOPAC, while highly reliable, comes with high costs and often operates within closed ecosystems requiring proprietary software (Montgomery, Nair, Chen, & Dikker, 2024; Wagner et al., 2021).

text.text: In contrast, an open-source device like B3 offers affordability, flexibility, and transparency, allowing researchers to access raw data in real time without relying on opaque algorithms (Montgomery et al., 2024).

text.text: This transparency supports open science practices and reproducibility by enabling researchers to inspect, validate, modify, and share signal-processing methods, including custom HRV analysis pipelines and artifact-removal techniques.
Moreover, the low cost of B3 means that laboratories with limited budgets, as well as large-scale requiring many sensors, to deploy multiple units without prohibitive expense.
The ability to integrate B3 with other open-source tools and software, since it is not locked into a single vendor's ecosystem, further enhances its utility for multi-modal experiments.
In our case, we further encourage integration in existing lab settings via the LSL platform with which B3 is fully compatible.
Notably, the present study demonstrates that these open source advantages need not come at the cost of data quality.

By showing comparable data quality across HR, HRV, and respiratory measures, these results support the use of B3 for scientific data collection in psychophysiology, exercise science, human-computer interaction, and related fields.
Moreover, the present results help establish confidence in the use of open-source devices in contexts that have historically relied upon commercial equipment.

Just as the EmotiBit project and others have aimed to "bridge the gap" between user-friendly wearables and high-fidelity research tools (Montgomery et al., 2024), the B3 adds to this movement by proving that an open hardware approach can meet the standards of physiological signal monitoring demanded by research applications.

text.text: The present findings provide a validation of B3 as an open-source platform for ECG and respiration recording.Several directions remain for future development and testing.

From an engineering perspective, future versions of B3 could further improve motion-artifact resistance, for example by using accelerometer or gyroscope data to reduce movement-related noise in the ECG signal during dynamic tasks.

The dual respiration setup (belt and thermistor) could also be further exploited by combining belt-and thermistor-based signals in a sensor-fusion approach, potentially improving the precision of respiration timing estimates.

In addition, although the present study focused on ECG and respiration, B3's open-source architecture could be extended to other physiological signals, such as electroencephalography (EEG) or EMG, provided that each new module is separately validated.
Future studies should also formally assess userexperience factors, including comfort, ease of setup, battery life, and suitability for longer recordings.
The present study validated individual B3 units rather than the multi device group configuration that ultimately motivates the platform.

Establishing the measurement performance of individual units was a necessary first step; however, future studies should assess the reliability, synchronization, and practical deployment of multiple B3 devices during interactive and ecologically valid experiments.

The ability to record sound synchronously with cardiac and respiratory signals, together with the possibility of using multiple devices simultaneously, makes B3 particularly suitable for studies of interpersonal dynamics, joint action, and music cognition.
For example, B3 could be used to examine physiological synchrony in dyads, small groups, ensemble musicians, dancers, choirs, or concert audiences.
The modest sample cannot fully represent variability across body types, age groups, or clinical populations.

Future validations should include a larger and more diverse sample, both to confirm B3's accuracy across different body types, ages, or clinical conditions, and to ensure that the device performs well for individuals with varied signal characteristics.
Another limitation is that the tasks, while covering a range of activities, were relatively short in duration.
Moreover, future studies could examine the durability of signal quality over time and under conditions like perspiration or prolonged motion, which can affect sensor adhesion and noise.

The comparative analysis indicates that the B3 open-source device is capable of delivering ECG and respiratory measurements with accuracy close to a widely used commercial system under variety of typical testing conditions.
Minor differences observed (a slight increase in motion artifacts during rapid arm movement, and a timing offsets in one respiratory sensor) did not undermine the overall data integrity.
The successful validation of B3 holds promise for the broader adoption of open-source physiology monitors.

By providing an affordable, transparent, and flexible alternative to proprietary systems, devices like B3 can empower a wider range of researchers and clinicians to collect high-quality physiological data.

This democratization of technology can accelerate scientific discovery and educational projects, as more groups are able to engage in biosignal research without the hurdle of prohibitive equipment costs.

text.text: The system is unique in that it can also record ambient sounds synchronously together with other physiological signals.
This makes B3 an ideal platform for running experiments in which auditory signals play a critical role, such as in research on speech and music perception and performance.
Moreover, the ability to deploy multiple devices simultaneously allows researchers to study group behavior.
Drawing on existing open hardware principles, B3 employs readily available electrical components and a custom-printed microcontroller circuit board to capture physiological signals.
As a consequence, the device can be built in any reasonably equipped workshop from parts that can be ordered from local or online electronics retails.
Beyond streaming the signals wirelessly in real time, B3 stores data on a Secure Digital (SD) memory card for offline analysis.
The open-source nature of B3's firmware and software pipeline lowers the barrier for researchers to adapt the platform to specialized tasks and to integrate real-time feedback or custom analytics.
By focusing on flexibility and user-friendliness, B3 aims to enable rapid prototyping of physiological experiments both in the lab and in real-world field settings.

LSL is an open-source middleware designed for unified, real-time collection and synchronization of time series data in research experiments (Kothe et al., 2024).
Using LSL in this context allows the device to be readily inserted into existing lab testing pipelines that already use this standard.

Although standard LSL recording software could be used, we also created a custom software application developed in MATLAB R2018a (version 9.4.0; The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) was used to acquire data in real time through the LSL protocol.

Its intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) allows users to visualize and record physiological signals simultaneously, while a companion suite of MATLAB and Python scripts handles post-experiment extraction, synchronization, and analysis of the recorded data (more details in GitLab (CRITIAS, 2026)).
